c.tagline: Belgium's canal-laced university city of medieval towers, vegetarian cuisine, and student energy.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered with regulated rates; most rides are booked by phone, app, or picked up at a taxi stand rather than hailed on the street.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU number reaching police, fire, and ambulance; 101 is the direct Belgian police line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the Korenmarkt, Patershol and festival crowds, especially during the Gentse Feesten; watch bikes and bags near Gent-Sint-Pieters station at night.

hood_desc: A maze of narrow medieval streets just north of Gravensteen castle, packed with some of Ghent's best restaurants and bars in restored gabled houses; ideal for food lovers who want to be steps from the main sights.
The pedestrianized heart of Ghent around the Belfry, Saint Bavo's Cathedral, and the Graslei/Korenlei waterfront; the natural base for first-timers who want everything walkable.
The lively student strip near Ghent University's main campus, lined with bars and late-night venues; suits younger travelers who want an energetic, budget-friendly nightlife scene.
A historic market square once the site of public gatherings and executions, now ringed by cafes, breweries, and independent shops; good for travelers who enjoy markets and craft-beer culture.
A quieter, redeveloped waterfront district along the old docks, with a marina, parks, and new housing; suits travelers seeking a calmer, residential feel away from the tourist core.

water.note: Tap water is safe and of high quality throughout Belgium.

transit.hours: Trams and buses generally run from about 5:00 AM to midnight, with a limited weekend night-bus network filling the gap.
transit.pay: Pay with a rechargeable De Lijn card, the De Lijn app, or contactless bank card tap-in on trams and buses; single paper tickets bought on board cost more.
transit.note: Ghent's compact center is best explored on foot or by bike; De Lijn trams and buses cover the wider city, and Gent-Sint-Pieters station links to Brussels and beyond by rail.

transit.m: Direct train to Gent-Sint-Pieters (~50 min, hourly)

tip.r: Service is included by law in restaurant and cafe bills; rounding up or leaving about 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Gentse waterzooi
food.desc: Ghent's creamy stew of chicken or fish with leek, carrot and potato in an egg-and-cream broth - the city's signature dish.

places.name: Meme Gusta
places.note: Vintage-styled Flemish kitchen built on family recipes; unpretentious and popular.

places.name: De Graslei
places.note: Waterside dining on the medieval quay, strong on the Ghent classics.

places.name: t Oud Clooster
places.note: Candlelit former chapel serving Flemish comfort food; small, so book ahead.

food.name: Gentse stoverij
food.desc: Beef slowly braised in dark Belgian ale with onions, mustard bread and a touch of syrup, served with a mountain of fries.

places.name: t Oud Clooster
places.note: Atmospheric candlelit room and a properly sticky beer stew.

places.name: Het Waterhuis aan de Bierkant
places.note: Canal-side beer cafe with over a hundred Belgian beers to drink with the stew.

places.name: Meme Gusta
places.note: Home-style stoverij from a kitchen that cooks the way grandmothers did.

food.name: Frieten met stoofvleessaus
food.desc: Twice-fried Belgian chips in a paper cone, topped with stew gravy or a thick sauce, eaten standing up at a street frituur.

places.name: Frituur Jozef
places.note: Long-running chip stand on the big square; classic cone with stoofvleessaus.

places.name: Frituur Bij Sint-Jacobs
places.note: Neighbourhood frituur beside the church and weekend flea market.

places.name: Korenmarkt frituren
places.note: Late-night chip stands in the middle of the bar district.

food.name: Cuberdons (Gentse neuzekes)
food.desc: Cone-shaped raspberry-purple sweets with a firm shell and syrupy centre, nicknamed little noses and sold from rival market carts.

places.name: Confiserie Temmerman
places.note: Old-fashioned sweet shop by the Patershol, full of Ghent confectionery.

places.name: Groentenmarkt neuzekes carts
places.note: Two rival purple carts side by side, each claiming the better cuberdon.

places.name: Huis van Alijn shop
places.note: Museum shop stocking Ghent sweets and other local edible souvenirs.

food.name: Tierenteyn mustard
food.desc: Sharp, freshly ground mustard scooped from a barrel into stoneware pots, made to a secret recipe since 1790 and eaten with everything.

places.name: Tierenteyn-Verlent
places.note: The original 1790 shop; mustard still ladled from the wooden cask.

places.name: Groot Vleeshuis
places.note: Medieval meat hall now an East Flanders produce house and tasting bar.

places.name: Het Waterhuis aan de Bierkant
places.note: Serves the mustard with cheese and sausage beer snacks across the water.

food.name: Mastellen and Gentse mokken
food.desc: Cinnamon-scented mastellen buns and hard aniseed mokken biscuits, sold from bakeries and stalls, especially around the Gentse Feesten.

places.name: Bakkerij Himschoot
places.note: Baking since 1880; queues for warm mastellen and cinnamon buns.

places.name: Confiserie Temmerman
places.note: Traditional Ghent biscuits and sweets alongside the cuberdons.

places.name: Vrijdagmarkt market stalls
places.note: Friday and Saturday market traders sell mokken and other old Ghent baking.

food.name: Ghent beer and Gruut
food.desc: Belgian abbey and sour ales plus Gruut, brewed in the city with herbs instead of hops - each style poured in its own glass.

places.name: Het Waterhuis aan de Bierkant
places.note: Canal-side beer cafe with a huge list and a terrace over the water.

places.name: Dulle Griet
places.note: Famous for the Max beer served in a horn glass; you leave a shoe as deposit.

places.name: Stadsbrouwerij Gruut
places.note: City brewery and taproom making hop-free herb beers you cannot get elsewhere.

food.name: Jenever
food.desc: Belgian juniper spirit, served ice cold and neat, in dozens of fruit and spice infusions from tiny specialist bars.

places.name: t Dreupelkot
places.note: Jenever-only bar beside the canal with more than 200 bottles behind the counter.

places.name: Het Waterhuis aan de Bierkant
places.note: Next door to the jenever bar; easy to move between beer and spirits.

places.name: Dulle Griet
places.note: Keeps a jenever selection alongside the beer list on the old square.

landmarks: Gravensteen (Castle of the Counts)
A moated 12th-century fortress rising improbably in the city centre, its battlements, torture museum and rooftop views straight from a medieval epic.
St Bavo's Cathedral and the Ghent Altarpiece
This soaring Gothic cathedral guards van Eyck's 1432 Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, the most stolen and most influential painting in art history.
Belfry of Ghent (Het Belfort)
The UNESCO-listed 91-metre civic tower, crowned by a gilded dragon, has sounded Ghent's pride since 1380 and rewards climbers with panoramic views.
Graslei and Korenlei
Ghent's gorgeous medieval harbour, where gabled guildhalls reflect in the Leie and students crowd the quaysides at golden hour.
St Michael's Bridge (Sint-Michielsbrug)
The classic viewpoint where Ghent's three towers — St Nicholas, the Belfry and St Bavo's — align in a single unforgettable medieval panorama.
St Nicholas' Church (Sint-Niklaaskerk)
A masterpiece of blue-grey Tournai stone in Scheldt Gothic style, its central lantern tower flooding the 13th-century crossing with light.
Patershol
A cobweb of cobbled medieval lanes behind the Gravensteen, once home to leather tradesmen and now Ghent's most atmospheric restaurant quarter.
Werregarenstraat (Graffiti Street)
An ever-changing legal graffiti alley where Ghent's street artists repaint the walls daily, linking the city's medieval fabric to its creative present.
Vrijdagmarkt
Ghent's historic gathering square, dominated by a statue of rebel leader Jacob van Artevelde, has hosted markets, executions and celebrations since the Middle Ages.
STAM (Ghent City Museum) and Bijloke Site
A medieval abbey and hospital complex ingeniously converted into the city museum, whose giant walk-on aerial map of Ghent is irresistible.

train.note: No international trains stop at Ghent - for Eurostar to London or Paris you change at Brussels-Midi, about 30 minutes away, and Lille in France is reachable with a change at Kortrijk. Gent-Sint-Pieters is the main station, a tram ride south of the centre, with very frequent domestic services to Brussels, Bruges (25 minutes) and Antwerp. Belgian fares are fixed-price with no advance discount.

bus.note: Coaches stop at Gent-Dampoort and Sint-Pieters. FlixBus runs to Brussels, Amsterdam, Paris and London, with the UK services including a full immigration check at the Channel - carry your passport. De Lijn buses and trams cover the city and the surrounding towns.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry. Ghent's canals carry sightseeing boats through the medieval centre and the Ghent-Terneuzen canal is a commercial waterway. International sailings leave from Zeebrugge, about an hour away.

half.name: Bruges
half.blurb: Canal-laced medieval city with cobbled squares and Gothic architecture, about an hour west of Ghent.

half.name: Antwerp
half.blurb: Flemish port city known for its Gothic cathedral, diamond district, and Rubens House museum.

half.name: Brussels
half.blurb: Belgium's capital, home to the ornate Grand Place square and the EU institutions, less than an hour away.
